tier_reason: These are first-party Criterion numbers from the README table. The benchmark code is public (benches/comparison.rs), and the repo's .cargo/config.toml pins the AVX2 rustflags. But no CPU model or rustc version is stated, and the current bench no longer matches the README's 1M-item setup, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Times are per Criterion iteration of 1,000 lookups (README table). Negative lookups: ~1.17 µs for bloomsday vs ~2.81 µs for sbbf-rs. Positive lookups: ~1.26 µs vs ~2.93 µs. The README headline says '~2.3x faster than sbbf-rs'. Per row, that is ~2.4x for negative and ~2.3x for positive lookups, or roughly 1.2 ns vs 2.8 ns per lookup (derived from page data).
corrections.workload: The README says 1,000,000 items at a 0.01 false-positive rate. The bench present when the table was written (first commit 3e3c423a, 2026-02-04) built both filters from 1M xxh64 hashes of random 16-character strings. Each Criterion iteration timed 1,000 pre-hashed negative lookups and 1,000 positive lookups. The current benches/comparison.rs (since commit ea15abbb) uses only 10,000 random u64 hashes, which is a cache-resident ~12.5 KB filter. So `cargo bench` at HEAD no longer reproduces the README setup. Both filters are sized the same way: ceil(-ln p / ln^2 2) = 10 bits per key, in 256-bit blocks.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Rust (rustc version not stated), Criterion 0.7, edition 2024. The repo's .cargo/config.toml applies rustflags to `cargo bench`. When the README table was written they were `-C target-feature=+avx2,+fma -C target-cpu=haswell`. They were changed to `target-cpu=native` in commit ea15abbb. The README does not say which configuration produced the published numbers.
corrections.caveats: The baseline is one specific Rust SBBF crate (sbbf-rs 0.2.8), not a hand-optimized C/C++ Bloom filter. The bench calls sbbf-rs through FilterFn, which holds a `&'static dyn FilterImpl`. That means one virtual call per lookup, while bloomsday's may_match_hash is inlined into the loop. Part of the gap is likely dispatch overhead rather than the filter layout. No CPU model is stated. The current bench uses a 10k-entry filter, not the README's 1M. A fastbloom comparison was added to the bench (commit bcd7cb84) and later removed (2de41178), and its results were never published. MIT is declared only in Cargo.toml: there is no LICENSE text file and GitHub detects no license. The README's `bloomsday = "0.1.0"` install line does not work, because the crate is not on crates.io. The project is only days old (all commits 2026-02-04 to 2026-02-06).

notes: The README numbers match the record. The record's doubt about flags was misplaced: the repo's .cargo/config.toml hardcodes the AVX2 rustflags, so `cargo bench` applies them. The real problems are elsewhere: the current bench shrank to 10k entries, and the sbbf-rs wrapper pays a dyn-dispatch call per lookup. License handling follows the existing precedent of treating a Cargo.toml-only MIT as copyable.

tier_reason: The only evidence is the author's own README and crate-doc statements: ~30% less space than Bloom filters and 'faster to query', with no dataset, hardware or measured Bloom comparison. The repo's benches (uniform.rs, nonuniform.rs, matrix_ops.rs) do not include a Bloom filter. These are numbers without methodology, so C.

corrections.caveats: There are no benchmark numbers, dataset or methodology behind the query-speed or construction-time claims. The repo's Criterion benches contain no Bloom filter baseline. The '~30% less space' figure matches the theoretical gap between a static-function filter at log2(1/ε) bits per key and a Bloom filter at ~1.44·log2(1/ε). ApproxSet defaults to 8 bits per entry, so ε ≈ 2^-8 (derived, not stated on page). Ribbon and xor filters achieve similar savings. The crate docs add only that queries take 'typically around 100-200 cycles if the map is in cache', and that building 100M entries takes ~2 minutes and 8 GB on an Apple M1. The author calls it research-grade ('Don't deploy it in production'), and it depends on bincode 2.0.0-RC.1. There have been no commits since 2022-11-23.

notes: The quote is verbatim in the README's Approximate sets section, and lib.rs repeats the ~30% space claim. The metadata is correct: MIT via LICENSE.txt, 51 stars, not a fork, not archived, and last commit 2022-11-23. pushed_at of 2023-03-30 is not a commit on master. The entry is metric=memory with only a qualitative speed claim, so it is borderline for a 'faster' catalog, but it is kept as tier C.

tier_reason: This is a first-party suite by the same author. The code is public (mpope9/exor_bechmark lib/exor_benchmark.exs), and the page states the CPU (i5-7267U) and Elixir/OTP versions. The measured C NIF's compiler and flags are not stated on the page (only Makefile defaults), and erbloom's Rust build is unstated. The script also has a sizing bug, so it stays C. The downgrade is for the overstated ratios, not the tier.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Figures are Benchee average time per 10,000 lookups. At 1M: fuse8 1.42 ms (705.73 ips) vs Bloomex 8.87 ms, Blex 13.17 ms and erbloom 4.01 ms, which is 6.26x, 9.29x and 2.83x (derived from page data, ips ratios). At 10M: fuse8 1.54 ms (648.42 ips) vs Bloomex 15.24 ms and Blex 18.47 ms, which is 9.88x and 11.98x (derived from page data). The page's 'erbloom 10M' row (3.90 ms, 2.53x derived) is invalid, because the script builds that filter from the 10k-key list. The page's Benchee 'x slower' figures (6.69x, 9.94x, 3.03x, 11.50x, 13.93x, 2.95x) are measured against the fastest row, fuse8 over a 100-element filter, not against the same-size fuse8.
corrections.workload: Benchee (mpope9/exor_bechmark, lib/exor_benchmark.exs; warmup 2 s, time 5 s) builds each filter over the integer keys 1..N, for N = 100, 1k, 100k, 1M and 10M. Each iteration then looks up keys 1..10,000, which are all positive lookups for N >= 10k. The fuse8 filters are built with `:none`, so their lookups skip erlang:phash2 on each key. The xor8/xor16 filters use default hashing, and the Bloom libraries hash internally. The Bloom libraries are Bloomex (pure Elixir, scalable, error 0.1), Blex (Erlang atomics, 0.01) and erbloom (Rust NIF, 0.1). efuse_filter is pinned in mix.lock at commit 7fc2c2d (2021-08-07). The 'erbloom 10M' filter is actually created from the 10k list (create_erbloom(bin10k)).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Elixir 1.12.2 and Erlang/OTP 24.0.5, per the Benchee output. efuse_filter is a C NIF wrapping FastFilter's binaryfusefilter.h, not Rust. Its c_src/Makefile defaults on macOS to `cc -O3 -std=c99 -arch x86_64 -finline-functions`, and the compiler version is not stated. erbloom is the Rust NIF, and its build profile is not stated.
corrections.caveats: The benchmark suite (exor_bechmark, 0 stars, no license) is by the same author as efuse_filter and exor_filter. It ran on a laptop, which the page itself flags as 'not a production environment'. Only fuse8 gets pre-hashed keys (`:none`), which skips erlang:phash2 on every lookup, while the other rows hash. Bloomex and Blex are pure Elixir/Erlang, so most of the 6-12x gap over them is C NIF vs BEAM code. The fairest baseline is erbloom, the Rust NIF: ~2.8x at 1M (derived). The erbloom 10M row is really a 10k-key filter. The Bloom filters were configured at looser FPRs (0.1 or 0.01) than fuse8's ~0.4%. Lookups are positive-only, on sequential integer keys. The hex.pm package has a single 0.1.0 release (2021-08-08).
corrections.stars_or_usage: 7 stars; hex.pm efuse_filter 0.1.0 (only release, 2021-08-08), 298 all-time downloads

notes: The ms and ips values are on the page, but most of the record's ratios came from Benchee's comparison column, which is relative to 'fuse8 100' rather than the same-size fuse8. Of the record's ratios, only erbloom 1M (2.8x) was a correct same-size ratio. The record also wrongly called the NIF Rust; it is C.
